title: Filtering Data: WHERE, Operators & Pattern Matching — Narration Scripts

lecture.New_Day3Part1audio01.mp3: The WHERE clause is the core row-level filter in SQL. The database evaluates the boolean condition in WHERE for every candidate row coming from the FROM clause. Only rows where the condition evaluates to TRUE pass through — any row evaluating to FALSE or NULL is filtered out.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio02.mp3: Here is the minimal WHERE clause structure. First, write SELECT followed by your desired columns. Next, write FROM followed by the table name. Finally, write WHERE followed by your filtering condition — for example, WHERE salary is greater than eighty thousand.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio03.mp3: Execution order is crucial: in SQL, WHERE runs as Step 2 — right after FROM, but before GROUP BY, HAVING, and SELECT. This means WHERE cannot reference column aliases defined in the SELECT list, because those aliases do not exist yet at filtering time.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio04.mp3: SQL provides six core comparison operators to build WHERE conditions. Let's explore each one.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio05.mp3: The equals operator checks for an exact match. Not equal, written as less-than greater-than or exclamation-equals, tests for inequality. Greater than and less than test numerical and date boundaries. Greater than or equal and less than or equal include the boundary value itself in your results.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio06.mp3: Here are comparison operators in action. The first query retrieves employees with a salary exceeding sixty thousand. The second finds products where stock quantity is zero or less. The third uses not equal to filter out a specific department.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio07.mp3: When you need to combine multiple conditions, SQL provides three fundamental logical operators: NOT, AND, and OR.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio08.mp3: The NOT operator inverts a condition: NOT TRUE becomes FALSE, and NOT FALSE becomes TRUE. Use it to cleanly exclude specific values or negate complex filters.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio09.mp3: The AND operator returns TRUE only when both conditions are met at the same time. If even one condition is FALSE, the entire AND filter evaluates to FALSE.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio10.mp3: The OR operator returns TRUE as long as at least one condition is met. Both conditions must be FALSE for the OR filter to fail.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio11.mp3: Operator precedence dictates the evaluation order: NOT evaluates first, followed by AND, and then OR. Because AND binds before OR, always use parentheses when combining AND with OR to make your logic crystal clear and prevent subtle bugs.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio12.mp3: Here are logical operators in practice. The first query uses AND to find active employees in department twenty. The second uses OR to find customers in the North or South region. The third uses NOT with LIKE to exclude a specific name pattern.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio13.mp3: Here is a critical trap: whenever NULL is involved in any comparison, the result is UNKNOWN — not TRUE and not FALSE. Because WHERE strictly requires a TRUE result to include a row, rows comparing against NULL are discarded. Always use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to explicitly test for missing values.

questions.New_Day3Question01.mp3: Ready to filter by price? Retrieve the name and unit price of all products with a price greater than ten thousand. Sort the results by unit price descending.
questions.New_Day3Question01sol.mp3: Let's write this query. SELECT name, unit price... FROM products... WHERE unit price is greater than ten thousand... ORDER BY unit price DESC. The WHERE clause filters out all products at or below ten thousand, and ORDER BY arranges the remaining products from most expensive to least.
questions.New_Day3Question02.mp3: Time to filter by region! Retrieve first name, last name, and region for customers in either the North or East region. Use the IN operator.
questions.New_Day3Question02sol.mp3: Here is the solution. SELECT first name, last name, and region... FROM customers... WHERE region IN North comma East. The IN operator is a clean alternative to chaining multiple OR conditions — it checks whether the region matches any value in your list.
questions.New_Day3Question03.mp3: Let's practice the BETWEEN operator! Find employees earning between sixty thousand and one hundred thousand inclusive. Retrieve first name, last name, and salary.
questions.New_Day3Question03sol.mp3: Let's code this. SELECT first name, last name, and salary... FROM employees... WHERE salary BETWEEN sixty thousand AND one hundred thousand. BETWEEN is inclusive on both boundaries — it is equivalent to writing salary greater than or equal to sixty thousand AND salary less than or equal to one hundred thousand.
questions.New_Day3Question04.mp3: Time to search with pattern matching! Find all employees whose first name starts with the letter S. Retrieve first name, last name, and salary.
questions.New_Day3Question04sol.mp3: The solution uses the LIKE operator. SELECT first name, last name, and salary... FROM employees... WHERE first name LIKE quote S percent quote. The percent wildcard matches any sequence of characters — so S percent matches any name starting with S followed by any number of characters.
questions.New_Day3Question05.mp3: Let's combine two conditions with AND! Find active employees — where is active equals one — who are in department twenty. Retrieve first name, department ID, and salary.
questions.New_Day3Question05sol.mp3: Here is the query. SELECT first name, department ID, and salary... FROM employees... WHERE is active equals one AND department ID equals twenty. Both conditions must evaluate to TRUE for a row to pass. AND is the exact operator needed here because we want employees who are simultaneously active AND in department twenty.
questions.New_Day3Question06.mp3: Final challenge — NULL handling! Find all employees who have no commission assigned. Retrieve first name, last name, and commission.
questions.New_Day3Question06sol.mp3: The solution uses IS NULL. SELECT first name, last name, and commission... FROM employees... WHERE commission IS NULL. Critical rule: you cannot write commission equals NULL — that always produces UNKNOWN and discards every row. IS NULL is the only correct way to test for missing data in SQL.
